title: Stable p-power image of a commuting matrix space
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], with algebraic closure $\bar k$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Assume $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$. Let $n\geq1$, and let $W\subseteq\operatorname{Mat}_n(k)$ be a $k$-linear subspace of the matrix algebra [def-weil-matrix]. Assume $XY=YX$ for all $X,Y\in W$ and $X^p\in W$ for all $X\in W$. Define $W_r=\operatorname{span}_k\{X^{p^r}:X\in W\}$ for integers $r\geq0$. For every extension field $K/k$, identify $K\otimes_kW$ with its image in $\operatorname{Mat}_n(K)$. Then $$K\otimes_kW_r=\operatorname{span}_K\{Y^{p^r}:Y\in K\otimes_kW\}.$$ The descending sequence $(W_r)$ stabilizes at a subspace $W_\infty$ closed under $p$th powers. This subspace is precisely the set of matrices in $W$ diagonalizable over $\bar k$, and $\bar k\otimes_k W_\infty$ is precisely the set of diagonalizable matrices in $\bar k\otimes_k W$. No perfectness of $k$ is assumed; the spans, rather than the set-theoretic images of the semilinear power maps, are part of the assertion. Here matrix multiplication is $(AB)_{ij}=\sum_{h=1}^n A_{ih}B_{hj}$, a span consists of finite linear combinations, and diagonalizable means conjugate by an invertible matrix to a diagonal matrix. Scalar extension uses the tensor product of vector spaces [def-weil-module-base-change], with $(a\otimes X)_{ij}=aX_{ij}$.

proof.text: First fix the scalar-extension identifications. For any subspace $U\subseteq\operatorname{Mat}_n(k)$ choose a basis of $U$ and extend it to a basis of the matrix space. Tensoring this basis with $K$ identifies $K\otimes_k U$ with the span of the first basis vectors inside $\operatorname{Mat}_n(K)$. The coordinate functional of any remaining basis vector vanishes on this span. Consequently $X\in\operatorname{Mat}_n(k)$ lies in $K\otimes_k U$ exactly when $X\in U$. The same coordinates show that extension preserves dimensions and subspace inclusions. This also proves the asserted injectivity of the tensor-to-matrix map; no separability is involved.

source.place: Agent-supplied linear-algebra expansion of Proposition 17.80, printed p.378, semisimple subspace; additive Jordan preliminaries, p.376.

proof.text: Put $F(X)=X^p$. For commuting matrices the binomial expansion gives $(X+Y)^p=X^p+Y^p$, since the intermediate binomial coefficients vanish in characteristic $p$, and $(aX)^p=a^pX^p$. Iterate to obtain $(\sum_i a_iX_i)^{p^r}=\sum_i a_i^{p^r}X_i^{p^r}$. Bilinearity of multiplication shows that all members of $K\otimes W$ commute, so the same formula holds there. It gives the inclusion of the right-hand span in $K\otimes W_r$; the reverse inclusion follows by taking $Y=1\otimes X$ for each generator $X^{p^r}$ of $W_r$. Thus the scalar-extension identity holds for every $K/k$, without extracting roots in $K$. The case $r=0$ is the identity.

source.place: Agent-supplied linear-algebra expansion of Proposition 17.80, printed p.378, semisimple subspace; additive Jordan preliminaries, p.376.

proof.text: Because $F(W)\subseteq W$, each generator $X^{p^{r+1}}=(X^p)^{p^r}$ of $W_{r+1}$ lies in $W_r$. The formula of step 2 also proves $W_{r+1}=\operatorname{span}_k F(W_r)$: the $p$th power of any finite linear combination of the generators of $W_r$ is a linear combination of the generators of $W_{r+1}$, and each such generator is the $p$th power of $X^{p^r}\in W_r$. A strict inclusion lowers the dimension, a nonnegative integer at most $n^2$. Therefore an equality $W_R=W_{R+1}$ occurs, and the recurrence makes all later terms equal. Set $W_\infty=W_R$; the recurrence gives $F(W_\infty)\subseteq W_\infty$.

source.place: Agent-supplied linear-algebra expansion of Proposition 17.80, printed p.378, semisimple subspace; additive Jordan preliminaries, p.376.

proof.text: Now work only over $L=\bar k$ and write $U=L\otimes_k W$. This field is algebraically closed [def-weil-algebraic-closure], so its only algebraic extension is $L$ itself; hence $L$ is perfect in the sense of the cited lemma, and an algebraic closure of $L$ is $L$, so geometrically semisimple endomorphisms of $L^n$ are exactly the diagonalizable ones. Take a finite basis $T_1,\ldots,T_d$ of $U$. By [lem-sfb-additive-jordan-linear-compatibility], $T_i=S_i+N_i$ with commuting diagonalizable $S_i$ and nilpotent $N_i$. Choose $r_0$ with $p^{r_0}$ at least a nilpotence exponent for every $N_i$ (take $r_0=0$ when $d=0$). For $r\geq r_0$, step 2 gives $T_i^{p^r}=S_i^{p^r}$, which is diagonalizable in an eigenbasis of $S_i$. These powers commute with each other because the $T_i$ commute. Step 2 identifies $L\otimes W_r$ with their $L$-span. The following joint-eigenspace argument shows every element of that span is diagonalizable.

source.place: Preliminaries to Proposition 17.74, printed p.376, additive Jordan decomposition; Proposition 17.80, p.378, agent-supplied large-power calculation.

proof.text: For the finite family $A_i=T_i^{p^r}$ in step 4, diagonalizability implies that its generalized eigenspace for $\lambda$ equals its eigenspace: in diagonal coordinates $(A_i-\lambda)^m v=0$ says $(a_j-\lambda)^m v_j=0$, hence $(a_j-\lambda)v_j=0$, for every coordinate $j$. Its eigenspaces span $L^n$. Apply [lem-sfb-commuting-joint-generalized-eigenspaces-span] to this commuting family. The resulting intersections are ordinary joint eigenspaces and span $L^n$. Every linear combination of the $A_i$ acts as a scalar on each such intersection. Selecting a basis from the spanning set of joint eigenvectors therefore diagonalizes that linear combination. This covers the empty family as well, whose span is zero. In particular every element of $L\otimes W_r$, for $r\geq r_0$, is diagonalizable.

source.place: Agent-supplied specialization of the joint generalized-eigenspace spanning theorem to the commuting diagonalizable powers in Proposition 17.80, p.378; pinned Mathlib LinearAlgebra/Eigenspace/Pi.lean:194-201.

proof.text: Conversely let $X\in U$ be diagonalizable. Let $E$ be the span of $X,X^p,X^{p^2},\ldots$. All these matrices are diagonal in one eigenbasis of $X$, so every element of $E$ is diagonal and $F$ is injective on $E$. The power formula of step 2, with $F(W)\subseteq W$, gives $F(U)\subseteq U$, hence $E\subseteq U$, and gives $F(E)\subseteq E$. Choose a basis $C_1,\ldots,C_e$ of $E$. If $\sum a_i C_i^p=0$, choose $b_i\in L$ with $b_i^p=a_i$. Then $(\sum b_i C_i)^p=0$, so injectivity forces every $b_i$, hence every $a_i$, to vanish. Thus the $e$ vectors $C_i^p$ form another basis of $E$. Taking $p$th roots of coefficients in this latter basis shows $F(E)=E$. Iterating, $X=Y^{p^r}$ for some $Y\in E\subseteq U$, for every $r$. By step 2, $X\in L\otimes W_r$ for every $r$, in particular for $r=R$. This uses perfectness only for $L$, never for $k$.

source.place: Agent-supplied linear-algebra expansion of Proposition 17.80, printed p.378, semisimple subspace; additive Jordan preliminaries, p.376.

proof.text: Take $r\geq\max(R,r_0)$. Steps 4-5 show every element of $L\otimes W_\infty=L\otimes W_r$ is diagonalizable; step 6 gives the converse inclusion among elements of $U$. Thus $L\otimes W_\infty$ is exactly the diagonalizable subset of $L\otimes W$. For $X\in W$, geometric diagonalizability means diagonalizability of $1\otimes X$ in that subset, hence membership in $L\otimes W_\infty$. By the coordinate test of step 1 this is equivalent to $X\in W_\infty$. Together with steps 2-3 this proves every clause. When $W=0$ or $n=1$ the same formulas apply, with no nonzero-element or positive-dimension assumption.
